Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Vignette:
Rohan's eyes would often glaze over when he thought about his younger brother, Kumar, who had passed away suddenly three years ago. It was as if he was right back in that hospital room, feeling the same numbness and disbelieving horror. The anniversary of Kumar's death was approaching, and Rohan could feel the familiar dread creeping up on him. He had been dreading this day for weeks, mentally rehearsing all the terrible things that could happen to his loved ones, as if preparing himself for another tragedy would somehow make it more bearable. Rohan's wife, Nalini, had tried to be supportive, but he knew she was getting frustrated with his increasing irritability. He would lash out at her over small things, and then immediately regret it. His body seemed to react before his mind could catch up, leaving him feeling like a ticking time bomb. At work, he struggled to concentrate on his interior design projects, finding himself zoning out in the middle of meetings or snapping at colleagues. Rohan had been avoiding anything that reminded him of Kumar's passing, including funerals and cemeteries. He wouldn't even drive by the cemetery where Kumar was buried, taking a detour every time he needed to go to his parents' house. Talking about loss with others made him anxious, as if sharing their grief would somehow unleash his own pent-up emotions. When friends or family members tried to discuss their experiences of losing loved ones, Rohan would politely excuse himself, feeling like he was on the verge of unraveling. At home, Rohan's avoidance behaviors had taken a toll on his relationship with Nalini. They used to love hosting dinner parties and game nights, but now Rohan found excuses to avoid social gatherings, fearing that someone might bring up Kumar or ask about their family. He knew Nalini felt isolated and alone in her grief, but he couldn't seem to shake off the feeling of impending doom. As the anniversary approached, Rohan's flashbacks became more frequent. He would be working on a design project when suddenly, he was back in that hospital room, reliving the moment when the doctor delivered the news about Kumar's passing. His heart racing, his palms sweating, Rohan felt like he was living in a constant state of hypervigilance. It wasn't until Nalini sat him down and told him she couldn't take it anymore – that she needed her husband back – that Rohan realized he needed help. He was exhausted from trying to control his emotions, from avoiding anything that reminded him of Kumar's passing. For the first time in years, Rohan felt a glimmer of hope that maybe, just maybe, he could learn to live with his grief instead of letting it consume him. As he sat in the therapist's office, Rohan knew what brought him there: the desperate desire to break free from the suffocating grip of his memories and find a way to honor Kumar's memory without losing himself.
